How the AI is used

One model, five real-time reliability scores

A small MLP reads the residuals and Innovation/NIS of an independent, fixed-covariance "Shadow" EKF and outputs a 0–1 trust score per sensor × degree-of-freedom, every tick. It never touches the sensor values themselves — only how much the state estimator should trust each one.

01
LiDAR + IMU + Encoder
raw measurements, cross-checked against each other
02
Shadow EKF
fixed covariance — produces Innovation & NIS with no feedback loop to the AI's own past decisions
03
Reliability AI
ONNX MLP — outputs s_v / s_ω per sensor, trained on 3-seed comparison against 3 baselines
04
Smoothing + recovery gate
fast to distrust, slow & gated to trust again
05
Bounded R inflation
R = R₀·[1+α(1−s)] — feeds the Adaptive EKF, or a stock robot_localization filter

Not just a browser demo

Runs on a real ROS2 + Gazebo stack

Every number on this page comes from the actual robotics pipeline — ROS2 Humble, Gazebo Classic, a TurtleBot3 waffle_pi — not a simplified web reimplementation. This is a live capture of the dashboard mid wheel-slip fault.

Live capture, Gazebo simulation. `encoder s_v` repeatedly drops near 0 during slip while every other channel stays high — the Adaptive EKF (blue) tracks ground truth (black) through the same loop the Fixed EKF (red, dashed) drifts away from.

Beyond these four episodes

Where the AI doesn't win. On LiDAR-only faults and pure sensor noise/spikes, a plain rule often beats the AI — the Shadow EKF fuses all three sensors into one state, so a LiDAR fault leaks into the encoder's own innovation signal and the AI can't always tell which sensor is actually broken. A hybrid (rule-for-LiDAR) fix was built and tested; it made the net result worse, not better, and was not shipped. The Encoder Spike tab above is one such honest case, left in deliberately.
